# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 15 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 15 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_015_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 7

**1** "Why was she shown to me as an aged woman in the former visions, and now as a young woman?" **2** She replied: "Listen. The reason she appeared as an aged woman in the first two visions is that your spirit was old and already withering, and had no power left on account of your infirmities and doubts. **3** For just as an aged person who has no hope of growing young again expects nothing but to pass away — so you, worn out by the cares of this life, had given up on yourselves and were not being renewed by the Lord. But after he spoke to you through me, and you turned your hearts to him, you were renewed, your infirmity fell away, strength returned to you, and you grew young. **4** And when you see the tower become a single solid stone, it will also come to pass: all who have believed sincerely will be made one — one body, one mind, one spirit, one faith, one love. And then the tower will be complete, and all will rejoice together." **5** "I would also like to know," I said, "why the stones from the deep sea are compatible with those from dry land when placed in the building." **6** She replied, "Because they all heard and believed. The sea-stones were tested and refined through fire; the land-stones did not require such testing."

---

### Council Notes

The explanation of the Church's age-to-youth progression is the most psychologically rich passage in the Visions. The Church's appearance reflects the spiritual state of her community — as they repent and are renewed, she grows younger. This is a profound ecclesiology: the health of the visible community directly affects the face of the Church.

The unity formula of v. 4 — "one body, one mind, one spirit, one faith, one love" — is a Hermaic creed that parallels Ephesians 4:4-6. Love replaces "baptism" and "God/Father of all" — emphasizing the relational over the sacramental.

The fire-testing of the sea-stones (martyrs) vs. the natural goodness of land-stones (holy livers) articulates two legitimate paths to salvation — both equally incorporated into the tower.
